title: Lakashim
summary: The pulse of life that Ecstatics seek to ride.

claims.text: Ecstatics name the rhythm of living energy Lakashim and hold that it calls out to itself through other living channels.
In their teaching, fear comes from refusing life and clinging to ego, while kundalini longs to rise toward the divine.
Euoi, the cry of the maenads, is taught as a wordless circle of sound with power of its own, much like a mantra.

title: Sh'zar at the Grand Convocation
summary: Why the Cult's founder pressed for a seat among the Traditions.

claims.text: Hermetics call Sh'zar's stand at the Convocation a power grab aimed at the Order and at leading the new Traditions.
Ecstatics tell it otherwise: as one voice with a few followers, Sh'zar needed a full order behind the visions or committees would talk them away.
Sh'zar's disciples travelled through dreams and timeless places across the world, and Tantric magicians in India saw Lakashim at work in their practice.

title: The Sahajiya era
summary: The Cult from the 16th century to the Victorian age.

claims.text: As the Traditions settled, the Seers drew back to India and the Middle East and took the name Sahajiya, leaving western Europe to the Hermetics and the Chorus.
In Europe most of them lived as wandering seers and madmen, sheltered by beliefs that the insane were touched by God or demons, with Time sight to warn them off.
Spread in secret cells, the Sahajiya split along ideological lines, and Victorian morals and colonial pressure left them badly weakened.

title: Ojas
summary: Places where the world's illusion thins and pure potential leaks in.

claims.text: Ojas are spots in space where possibility breaks through; their energy, called Shakti or Kundalini, is held to build the universe.
Hard exercise can strengthen them, sex can align them between partners so power flows, and Tantric postures can focus them.
Ecstatics treat the spirit world as more truthful than the physical, since it mirrors the soul of people and land, cruel dreams and kind ones alike.

title: Fellowship of Pan
summary: Ecstatics devoted to human nature and wild joy.

claims.text: Their tale says the Fellowship began when humans and satyrs, born of human joy, embraced in the open countryside.
They accept that people are capable of love and senseless violence, but think humanity leans to virtue and is purest when lost in art, love or drink.
Members are skilled at healing, calming tempers and inspiring others, and dance binds them in fellowship with humans, spirits and fae.

title: Aghoris, Hagalaz and Acharne
summary: The Cult's brutal, barely tolerated factions.

claims.text: Mainstream Cultists, Joybringers above all, find these groups repellent, yet hard times have made them a grim necessity.
The Hagalaz answered Sh'zar's first call and stay loosely tied but fiercely loyal to their fellows.
The Aghoris have walked the path for thousands of years; the Acharne joined after the First World War posing as an occult society before showing their true practices.

title: Modern Ecstatic factions
summary: Why the Cult keeps spawning and shedding groups.

claims.text: The Cult must stay on the edge of its time, so it constantly gives birth to new factions and drops old ones; Klubwerks, for one, set old ideas to modern subcultures.
Loose discipline in the new factions opens the way to addiction and careless use of foci, against the Cult's stress on self-control.

title: Joybringers
summary: The mainstream faction of the Cult.

claims.text: Joybringers grew out of the Cult of Bacchus after it lost ground to the ideas of Nietzsche, Freud, Darwin and Marx; mystics among the rest went to the Fellowship of Pan.
They follow the Code of Ananda closely and work with the homeless, the sick, refugees and prisoners, even urging generals toward non-lethal arms.
Joybringers who fail to watch their indulgences risk becoming hooked on their own foci.
